cultural.vision_reason: A carved wooden wolf-head frontlet/mask with saw-teeth and painted eye sockets, a form consistent with Northwest Coast (Nuu-chah-nulth) ceremonial regalia; the object is clearly a ritual mask/forehead ornament as described.

physical.title: mask; forehead-ornament
physical.summary: Mask, or rather forehead frontlet, in the form of a wolf head, carved of two pieces of alder [?], upper and lower jaws. The surface of the exterior indicates fine adze/knife work; that in the interior is rather crude but strongly suggest the use of metal bladed 'D' adzes. The face is carved with a long muzzle, prominent snout with raised nostrils, low bridge to the muzzle, sweeping low forehead, with prominent curved lines above the eyes. The eyes are excavated ovoids, the orbits left remaining, the excavated area filled with white paint. The saw teeth, carved well into the mouth, point backwards into the mouth, on the bottom and top of the jaws. The red painted snout is excavated with two simple lines for nostrils. The head is painted black, except for the underside of the lower jaw, the snout as mentioned, and the chin. The teeth are painted white. The underside of the jaw has a central axis ridge ending in a flat triangular area on the underside of the back of the head. The forehead was originally fitted with a cedar bark [?] cape, for which there are three holes for attachment. The upper and lower jaws are secured through two pairs of holes, with two-ply 'Z' twist animal sinew cord. This, perhaps at the time of acquisition has been crossed over the snout and tied under the chin to stop the mask opening. Attached to the left hand side of the frontlet is a further piece of vegetal string, 'S' twist and possibly aboriginal.

cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a carved wooden human face mask with painted features and attached hair fringe, consistent with Northwest Coast (Nuu-chah-nulth) ceremonial mask traditions used in ritual dance.

physical.title: mask
physical.summary: Human face mask, carved of alder with prominent and extremely emphatic features. The domed forehead is separated, by very long raised black painted eyebrows, from flat planes descending to eyes deeply set into ovals, painted white with cut out ovoids for sight. A large hooked nose flows into raised cheeks below the eyes, with a great exaggerated, non-realistic faceted and black-painted surround emphasising the red-painted mouth. This feature may have been designed merely to accentuate the mouth area, but it is also possible that it represents mouth of a skin being worn by individual with the red painted mouth. The area between the two mouths is painted white. The nostrils are lightly excavated, with a grommet of cedar withe [?] below. Teeth have been added across the open mouth, splints, with a horizontal painted line to indicate the join between upper and lower jaw teeth. Most are missing. The black second mouth seems also to turn into a beard, with a vertical addition down the chin axis. The mask is otherwise painted haematite [?] red, with two black dots on the forehead above the nose. The edge and upper sides of the mask are decorated with pegged bunches of human hair, mostly missing from the right side. The centre bunches are tied together with a length of seaweed or skin thong. The surface of the mask is nicely finished with knife/adze work, and the interior indicates the shape of the narrow bladed adze [?] used to excavate the face area. Perhaps the most interesting feature of the mask is that the grommet has nearly been eaten away by the wearer; furthermore there is an arc shaped area of dirt in the place where one would expect sweat and saliva to accumulate from the wearer. The shinyness at the the chin and lower jaw is likely to have arisen by handling post-collection.

cultural.vision_reason: Red cedar dance mask with a mouth grommet for holding in the dancer's teeth is a classic Northwest Coast (Nuu-chah-nulth/Nootkan) ceremonial performance mask type, consistent with the claimed culture.

physical.title: mask
physical.summary: Face mask made of red cedar wood, with a triangular horizontal cross section, deeply carved interior to accomadate the face, lipped interior edges to the top and sides, and a grommet inserted under the nostrils so that the mask can be held by the dancer in the teeth. The rounded forehead is cut with a pair of large raised eyebrows, over deeply carved eye sockets, outlines with a second ridge above the eye, the eyes each being outlined with a raised flat area around pierced openings. The flat cheeks fall away towards a raised protuberant mouth, cut open and oval as though in the act of singing; the promiment rounded or Roman nose has nostrils carved underneath, visible to people sitting under the dancer. The forehead is painted dark red, the eyebrows, moustache and central chin black, with a further black dash on the wearers left cheek. The wood is taken from somewhere near the centre of a log, with the nose pointing into the heartwood, and the back edges of the mask towards the bark; this configuration means that the richly contoured grain is clearly visible.  There are no attachments at the forehead for cedar bark; there are two holes on each side for attachments, or more probably straps. The bottom is crudely hacked away; the grommet shows some sign of teeth marks.

2013.13.0007 Canada Pukmis mask av röd ceder. Föreställer "en drunknad som p g a sin andliga träning vaknar till liv igen". En blandning mellan människa och ande. Hår av växtmaterial.
Tillverkad av Tom Paul (Thomas Donald Maxwell Paul, son till Tim Paul), Nuu-Chah-Nulth (nootka), British Columbia. Masken beställdes av Etnografiska museet 2006/2007 och betalades med vektyg via Carl-Johan Gurt. Den blev klar 2013 och hämtades av Carl-Johan Gurt i juli 2013 och lämnades till museet oktober samma år. Nordvästkusten Nordvästkusten 02 Nordvästkustindianerna 02:2 2013.13.0007 Canada
